content: The Maternal, Child, and Adolescent Health and Ageing (MCA) department, along with the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety (NFS), prioritized updating the recommendation on zinc supplementation. This decision followed advice from the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) in response to new evidence regarding this intervention. The recommendation in this global guideline is intended to guide the development of national and local health policies and clinical protocols. The target audience includes national and local public health policymakers, managers of maternal and child health programs, non-governmental organizations, professional societies, health professionals (such as obstetricians, midwives, nurses, nutritionists, and general practitioners), researchers, and academic staff involved in training health professionals. The updated recommendation applies to all pregnant women and adolescent girls receiving antenatal care (ANC) in healthcare facilities or community-based settings, as well as their fetuses and newborns. This guideline question was prioritized during the WHO 2016 ANC guideline development process and was further prioritized for updating in 2019 as part of WHO’s living guideline commitment. The outcomes of interest remain consistent with those prioritized in the ANC guideline for nutritional interventions, including maternal outcomes (e.g., infections, anemia, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, gestational diabetes, mode of delivery, excessive weight gain, maternal mortality, and satisfaction) and fetal/neonatal outcomes (e.g., neonatal infections, small for gestational age, low birth weight, preterm birth, congenital anomalies, macrosomia, and fetal/neonatal mortality). This recommendation is an update of one of the 49 recommendations published in the WHO guidelines on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience. The development process followed standardized procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. This included identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for implementation, dissemination, and evaluation. The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) is an independent panel of external experts and stakeholders from the six WHO regions. This group advises WHO on prioritizing new and existing questions in maternal and perinatal health for guideline development or updating. The WHO Steering Group, comprising staff from the MCA, NFS, and SRH departments, managed the updating process. They drafted the priority question in PICO format, identified guideline methodologists and development group members, supervised evidence retrieval and synthesis, and finalized the guideline document. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) consisted of 12 external experts and stakeholders from the six WHO regions, ensuring representation, gender balance, and no significant conflicts of interest. These experts reviewed evidence, interpreted findings, and formulated the final recommendation during an online meeting on January 13, 2021. The GDG also reviewed and approved the final guideline document before submission to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The External Review Group (ERG) was a geographically and gender-balanced group of four members, including technical experts and stakeholders. They peer-reviewed the draft guideline document for factual accuracy, clarity, contextual issues, and implementation implications. The ERG ensured that the decision-making process incorporated the values and preferences of affected populations, including pregnant women, adolescent girls, healthcare professionals, and policymakers. The systematic review team, led by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group, coordinated the updating of the quantitative systematic review and facilitated collaboration between systematic review authors and guideline methodologists. Evidence was appraised using the GRADE methodology, assessing the certainty of evidence based on criteria such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Qualitative evidence was synthesized from studies on women’s and healthcare professionals’ views on ANC. This evidence was appraised using the GRADE-CERQual tool, which evaluates methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance to the review question. The evidence summary and profile were prepared using the DECIDE framework, which systematically considers research evidence on interventions based on six criteria: effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The GDG reviewed the evidence summary in advance of the online meeting, where they discussed and made judgments on the intervention’s impact for each criterion. The final recommendation was formulated through group discussion until consensus was reached. The guideline preparation process involved drafting a full document to reflect the deliberations and decisions of participants. A preliminary version was electronically shared with participants and the ERG for final review and technical comments.
